title: Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency and NICT roll out Kyukyu VoiceTra, a 15-language speech-translation app for ambulance crews, to fire headquarters nationwide
summary: Kyukyu VoiceTra, a speech-translation app for ambulance crews, reached 690 of Japan's 720 fire headquarters by 1 January 2025; more than 70% of Sapporo crews said that it sped up communication.
account: NICT, the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology, announced on 18 April 2017 that Kyukyu VoiceTra would be provided to fire headquarters nationwide from that month. The speech-translation app for ambulance crews was developed with the Fire and Disaster Management Agency (FDMA) and its Fire Research Center on NICT's VoiceTra engine. It adds medical terms to improve the accuracy of free-text translation. It also adds 46 fixed phrases for emergency scenes in 15 languages. The Sapporo Fire Department had used it since February 2017. The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' 2017 white paper covers the research and development, part of the action plan toward 2020. It records completion as Kyukyu VoiceTra in April 2017 and the start of provision to all fire headquarters. Its download figures (205,421 by the end of fiscal 2015 and 621,221 by the end of fiscal 2016) are for the general VoiceTra app. The trade publication risktaisaku.com (8 May 2017) described the Android release and a planned iOS version. It also described on-screen text that helps communication with hearing-impaired patients. The Fire Research Center and NICT developers wrote in September 2017 that more than 70% of Sapporo ambulance crews said in a survey that the app made communication faster and better than existing methods. More than 90% wanted to keep using it. The developers also wrote that 180 fire headquarters had started using the app by 7 August 2017. Their own field tests of the general VoiceTra app had found that translated exchanges took about twice as long as exchanges in Japanese, which led them to add fixed phrases. Ninomiya Town's fire service announced its own adoption on 6 December 2022. By 1 January 2025, 690 of Japan's 720 fire headquarters (95.8%) used the app, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. No cited source documents an outcome for a patient.
purpose: Built to let ambulance crews communicate with foreign patients quickly at emergency scenes. No cited source documents an outcome for a patient.

developer: NICT (National Institute of Information and Communications Technology) with the Fire and Disaster Management Agency and its Fire Research Center
deployer: Fire headquarters across Japan (Sapporo Fire Department from February 2017; Ninomiya Town fire service from 2022)
segment: Ambulance crew communication with foreign patients
taxonomy_note: The intended good is that non-Japanese speakers can be understood by ambulance crews, a language-access gain rather than acceptance as such, and no outcome is measured.

fields.summary: Kyukyu VoiceTra, a speech-translation app for ambulance crews, reached 690 of Japan's 720 fire headquarters by 1 January 2025; more than 70% of Sapporo crews said that it sped up communication.
fields.account: NICT, the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology, announced on 18 April 2017 that Kyukyu VoiceTra would be provided to fire headquarters nationwide from that month. The speech-translation app for ambulance crews was developed with the Fire and Disaster Management Agency (FDMA) and its Fire Research Center on NICT's VoiceTra engine. It adds medical terms to improve the accuracy of free-text translation. It also adds 46 fixed phrases for emergency scenes in 15 languages. The Sapporo Fire Department had used it since February 2017. The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' 2017 white paper covers the research and development, part of the action plan toward 2020. It records completion as Kyukyu VoiceTra in April 2017 and the start of provision to all fire headquarters. Its download figures (205,421 by the end of fiscal 2015 and 621,221 by the end of fiscal 2016) are for the general VoiceTra app. The trade publication risktaisaku.com (8 May 2017) described the Android release and a planned iOS version. It also described on-screen text that helps communication with hearing-impaired patients. The Fire Research Center and NICT developers wrote in September 2017 that more than 70% of Sapporo ambulance crews said in a survey that the app made communication faster and better than existing methods. More than 90% wanted to keep using it. The developers also wrote that 180 fire headquarters had started using the app by 7 August 2017. Their own field tests of the general VoiceTra app had found that translated exchanges took about twice as long as exchanges in Japanese, which led them to add fixed phrases. Ninomiya Town's fire service announced its own adoption on 6 December 2022. By 1 January 2025, 690 of Japan's 720 fire headquarters (95.8%) used the app, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. No cited source documents an outcome for a patient.
